narrative: The model estimated your chance of becoming a bad credit risk at 36%. The bank treated that level of risk as too high for approval, so your application was denied. The decision came from a balance of factors. Your credit history was the most influential factor. It included critical or other credits, which appear in about a third of approved cases, and it actually worked in your favor by pulling the assessment toward good credit. The strongest negative signal was your checking account status. A negative balance is uncommon among approved applicants—only around one in eight had this—so it pushed your risk upward and outweighed the favorable credit-history effect. The third most important factor was the share of your disposable income going to installments. At 2%, it is below the approved average of about 3%, so it helped your case by suggesting your monthly payments are relatively manageable. To improve your chances, focus on bringing your checking account balance positive and keeping it stable. Reducing existing credit obligations and requesting a smaller amount, since your requested amount is well above the approved average, could also help. Ask the bank what specific evidence would update your file, then reapply once those records show a stronger repayment position.
